Monotonicity and \CFTP (old version)^[\textcolor{red}{THIS SECTION IS NOW SUPERSEDED}] {#sec-monotonicity-CFTP-OLD}
======================


Timeline features and the epidemic portrait {#sec:timeline-features}   {- .unlisted}
-------------------------------------------
Analysis of the four stages of the simplified "two-sweeps"
construction (@thm-simplified-construction) leads us
to identify 
features permitting a succinct description of the construction.
This will also facilitate a proof of monotonicity, central to \CFTP. 
Recall the notation of
Equations (-@eq-infections-collections,
-@eq-removals-collections, -@eq-removals-vectors) in @def-notation, and the notions of \ITP and
susceptible, infected and removed regions
in @def-epidemic-attributes.
For simplicity, assume throughout that \(R_{0-}{=}0\).

:::{.callout-caution #cau-removals-at-zero}
### Removals at zero
Revisit the assumption that \(R_0{=}0\)?
:::

Consider the initial \State at \algorithmictime zero:
\((\InnovRem{}^{(0)},\InnovInf{}^{(0)},I_{0-}{}^{(0)})\) yielding an epidemic with conditioned removals
occurring precisely at times \(t_1{<\ldots<}t_\TotalRemovals\) in \([0,\Duration)\):
\[
\InnovRemC{}^{(0)} \quad=\quad \left\{\CRemoval_{t_1}^{\target_1}\,, \ldots\, \CRemoval_{t_\TotalRemovals}^{\target_\TotalRemovals}\right\}\,.
\]
The first step in \algorithmictime is made using an \ExtendedInnovation
\((\InnovRemMarked{(*)}, \InnovInfMarkedA{(*)},I_{0-}^{(*)}, \InnovResampling^{(*)})\).
Note that attention need only focus on the first 
\(\TotalRemovals\) timelines. This is because
the remaining 
\(\Population{-}\TotalRemovals\) individuals remain susceptible throughout
the process-time interval \([0,\Duration)\) of interest,
thus playing no role in the development of the epidemic other than implicitly increasing
overall infection rates. 


**First stage** (replacing
the initial in\activated removals in \(\InnovRemR{}^{(0)}\)).
This is straightforward, because
_in\activated_ removals do not affect the process-time evolution of the epidemic,
so can be removed wholesale.
New potential removals from \(\InnovRemMarked{(*)}\)
can be introduced only if not immediately \activated, which is to say, if they do not lie in the infected region.
In fact we may and do additionally _disregard_ all proposed removals lying in the removed region
(this region is determined by the 
conditioned removal times \(t_1{<\ldots<}t_\TotalRemovals\), 
which are constant over all \algorithmictime).
Such potential removals cannot affect the algorithm at any stage.
So the first stage forms \(\InnovRemR{}^{(1)}\) by deleting all of 
\(\InnovRemR{}^{(0)}\)
(all current in\activated removals), and replacing them
by those new in\activated removals 
from \(\InnovRemMarked{(*)}\)
whose tuples of (time \(t\), target mark \(\target\)) lie
in the susceptible region. All replacements
are in\activated removals
but may later constrain new proposed infections.

We note in passing that \(\InnovRemMarked{(*)}\)
is a Poisson point process, so 
almost surely all new potential removal proposals
lie on straight components of the susceptible/infected region boundary.

**Second stage** (proposing target mark changes for conditioned removals):
the target marks of \(\InnovRemC{}^{(0)}\)
are re-sampled using proposals \(m_1{,\ldots,}m_\TotalRemovals\)
from \(\InnovResampling^*\). The target mark \(\target_r\) of \(\CRemoval_{t_r}^{\target_r}\)
is replaced by \(m_r\) if \(R < m_r \leq R+I\), where
\((S,I,R)\) is the \processstate in the epidemic \trajectory
corresponding to the incident \(\InnovRemC{}^{(0)}\) in the epidemic \history
incident list
(for \trajectory and \history defined in @def-epidemic-attributes).
This delivers the change from \(\InnovRemC{}^{(0)}\)
to \(\InnovRemC{}^{(1)}\).

:::{.callout-caution #cau-new-marks}
Be explicit here and at @thm-simplified-construction
about \(\InnovResampling^*\) delivering \(m_1{,\ldots,}m_\TotalRemovals\).
:::

It follows from these first two stages that after the first \algorithmictime step 
\[
\InnovRemMarkedR{\target}{}^{(1)} [t_\target,\Duration) \quad=\quad \emptyset\,,
\qquad 
\InnovRemMarkedC{\target}{}^{(1)} (t_\target,\Duration) \quad=\quad \emptyset\,;
\]
The equation for
\(\InnovRemMarkedR{\target}{}^{(1)} [t_\target,\Duration)\)
follows because we don't add in\activated removals to the removed region
(\(\InnovRemMarked{(*)}\)
is a Poisson point process, so no in\activated removals are proposed exactly at time \(t_\target\));
the equation for
\(\InnovRemMarkedC{\target}{}^{(1)} (t_\target,\Duration)\)
holds since conditioned removal must not be located in the removed region.
Likewise, no in\activated removals are added to initially infected timelines, so
\[
\InnovRemMarkedR{\target}{}^{(1)} \quad=\quad \emptyset \quad\text{for \(\target\le I_{0-}\).}
\] {#eq-no-pot-removals-on-initial-infective}

These first two stages exhibit a useful monotonicity: pointwise increase
of the \(R+I\) \trajectory (implying increase of the infected region) forces drop-out of
some of the replacement inactive removals
produced in stage 1 for \(\InnovRemMarkedR{\target}{}^{(1)}\),
while more stage 2 proposals for change of target mark
will be accepted (and these extra accepted proposals
will always be for mark increase).

**Third stage** (processing the \(\prec\)-ordered list of infections):
this is more involved. We may choose
\[
\InnovInfMarkedA{\infector<\infectee}{}^{(1)}(t_\infector,\Duration) \quad=\quad \emptyset\,,
\]
since \((t_\target, \Duration)\) belongs to the removed region;
any infections added there would never be \activated and so would never affect the course of the epidemic.
Generation of \(\InnovInfMarkedA{(1)}\) is based on two constructions:


:::{.callout-caution #cau-monotonicity-notes}
### \textcolor{red}{\textbf{TO HERE!!}}
Revision needed in this section after this point.
:::


* The _laziest feasible epidemic_ (\LFE). 
This can be informally described as the slowest possible epidemic 
that can be created by deleting potential infections while 
preserving the conditioned removals 
(and avoiding the activation of any potential removals, as always). 
The most transparent definition runs as follows:

   - consider all possible epidemics arising from the union of the \algorithmictime-\(0\) epidemic \history with a subset of those potential infections from \(\InnovInfMarkedA{\infector<\infectee}{}^{(1)}\) whose infectee marks remain at or below the \algorithmictime-\(0\) \(\ITP\);
   - restrict attention only to those epidemics which activate all the conditioned removals \(\InnovRemC{}^{(0)}\) (they won't activate any 
   removals in \(\InnovRemR{}^{(0)}\) because they have been chosen to lie below the \algorithmictime-\(0\) \(\ITP\));
   - there will be a slowest-possible epidemic among these (prove by mixing infections between different epidemics);
   - the \(\ITP\) of this slowest-possible epidemic forms the \(\LFE\).

* This \(\LFE\) can be characterized by an equation based on backwards-induction.

* It is also monotonic in the initial value and the \algorithmictime-\(0\) \(\ITP\) (use simple arguments about set-inclusion).

* The _no-fly zone_ (\NFZ\).
This can be informally described as the subset of \Timelinespace \(\TimeLineSpace\)
of points which, if infected, would entail activation of some in\activated removal from \(\InnovRemMarkedR{\target}{}^{(1)}\).

   - For each in\activated removal in \(\InnovRemMarkedR{\target}{}^{(1)}\) one can trace backwards in process-time a path of potential infections using \(\InnovInfMarkedA{\infector<\infectee}{}^{(1)}\), and omitting all infections which would connect to the \algorithmictime-\(0\) \(\ITP\)) **needs better description!**. 
   - Stop this once the path passes above a further in\activated removal in \(\InnovRemMarkedR{\target}{}^{(1)}\), in which case continue tracing backwards but starting from this new in\activated removal. The whole procedure ceases once process-time zero is achieved.
   
* This \(\NFZ\) can be characterized by an equation based on backwards-induction.

* It is also monotonic in the initial value and the \algorithmictime-\(0\) \(\ITP\) (use simple arguments about set-inclusion and an observation
that if an in\activated infection is made available in the higher rather than 
the lower \(\NFZ\)) then the higher \(\NFZ\)) must be strictly higher than
the lower).

* Finally observe the \algorithmictime-\(1\) \(\ITP\) depends
monotonically on the pair of \(\LFE\) and \(\NFZ\).

--------------------------------

Older remarks:

(a) Follow stage 3 of @thm-simplified-construction by working backwards through the \(\prec\)-ordered infections \chronology \(\Chronology_2\)
which is the result of \(\prec\)-sorting
\(\InnovInfMarkedA{(0)}\sqcup\InnovInfMarkedA{(*)}\);
(b) Consider only those \(\Infection_t^{\target<\infectee}\in\Chronology_2\)
with \((t,\target)\) not lying in the removed region;
(c) If a potential infection \(\Infection_t^{\target<\infectee}\)
comes from \(\InnovInfMarkedA{(0)}\) then retain it in \(\InnovInfMarkedA{(1)}\) only if
otherwise there would be a failure to activate one of the (possibly re-marked) conditioned removals
at times \(t_1{<\ldots<}t_\TotalRemovals\). In this case convert \(\Infection_t^{\target<\infectee}\) to a _perpetuated_ infection
\(\PInfection_t^{\target<\infectee}\);
(d) If a potential infection comes from \(\InnovInfMarkedA{(*)}\) then add it to \(\InnovInfMarkedA{(1)}\) only if
its addition would _not_ result in activation of one of the in\activated removals of \(\InnovRemMarkedR{(1)}\).

Suppose we have reached \(z=\Infection_t^{\target<\infectee}\) and are considering the impact of remark (c).
If \(z\) is not \activated in the epidemic of \algorithmictime \(\tau{=}0\) then its removal cannot damage the possibility of
infecting all the conditioned removals. 
If it _is_ \activated in the epidemic of \algorithmictime \(0\)
then \(\target\) must belong to the \(\tau{=}0\) removed region 
and \(\infectee\) must lie at the bottom of the \(\tau{=}0\) susceptible region.
Both of these are determined by \(z\) together with \(\InnovRemMarkedC{(0)}[0,z)\)
and \(\InnovInfMarkedA{(0)}[0,z)\): however \(\InnovRemMarkedC{(0)}[0,z)\) can be replaced by \(\InnovRemMarkedC{(1)}[0,z)\),

of removals and hence will not alter the infected and removed regions up to incident \(z\).
Removal of \(z\) will break the possibility of
infecting all the conditioned removals if the epidemic started at time \(t\) with initial \processstate \((S_{t-},I_{t-},R_{t-})\)
[(beware of times not incidents here! refer explicitly to]{.mark} \processstate, [and use \(\tau=0\))]{.mark}
and using \(\InnovRemMarked{(1)}[z,\Duration)\)
and \(\InnovInfMarkedA{(1)}[z,\Duration)\) fails to infect the conditioned removals in \(\InnovRemMarkedC{(1)}[z,\Duration)\).

**Work towards** the _laziest feasible epidemic_ (\LFE\): the lowest path of \activated infections
that would activate all the \(\TotalRemovals\) conditioned removals in \(\InnovInfMarkedA{(1)}\).
This can be created inductively while working backwards through \(\Chronology_2\).


* Step (d\)  can be efficiently implemented using the _no-fly zone_ (\NFZ\), the subset of \(\Timelinespace\)
of points which, if infected, would entail activation of some in\activated removal from \(\InnovRemMarkedR{\target}{}^{(1)}\).
This can also be created inductively while working backwards through \(\Chronology_2\).

:::{.callout-caution #cau-removals-not-times}
### Working with removals not times
:::


We now construct three useful regions of timeline-space, illustrated in @fig-NFZ-LFE. \label{use-of-timeline-space}

(Here and throughout we use the convention that \(\max\emptyset=-\infty\)
and \(\min\emptyset=\infty\).)\label{inequality-conventions}

The first of these is the _no-fly zone_ (\NFZ): this is made up of initial portions of timelines, with the no-fly zone on timeline \(\infectee\) being written as \([-\infty,\nfz^\infectee]\), where \(\nfz^\infectee\) is defined in @def-no-fly-zone below. 
The \NFZ is the zone within which 
infection of a timeline point would result (later in process-time) in the activation of a previously in\activated removal, thus breaking the conditioning
that removals are \activated only at \(t_1{<\ldots<}t_\TotalRemovals\).

There are two possible ways in which this might occur: 

1. either the infection might activate a hitherto in\activated removal on timeline \(\infectee\); 

2. or (if \(\infectee{<}\TotalRemovals\)) the infection might activate a hitherto in\activated infection of a higher timeline in the no-fly zone,
which would lead inductively to activation of an in\activated removal (perhaps on a still higher timeline).

The first consideration leads to the requirement that \(\nfz^\infectee\) must lie to the right 
of all in\activated removals with target mark \(\infectee\). This leads to
\(\nfz^\infectee\geq\max\{t: \Removal_t^\infectee\in\InnovRemMarkedR{\infectee}\}\).
(Bear in mind that we deem \(\InnovRemMarkedR{\infectee}[t_\infectee,\Duration)=\emptyset\).)
However this strengthens to 
\(\nfz^\infectee\geq\max_{r\leq \infectee}\max\{t: \Removal_t^r\in\InnovRemMarkedR{r}\}\).
because infection of timeline \(\infectee\) at time \(t\) can happen only if there are prior infections
of timelines lower than timeline \(\infectee\).

The second consideration (applying only when \(\infectee{<}\TotalRemovals\)) leads inductively to the 
requirement that \(\nfz^\infectee\) must lie to the right of all in\activated infections with target mark \(\target\) and infectee mark
\(\infectee{+}1\) timed at or before both \(\nfz^{\infectee+1}\) and \(t_\target\).
So
\(\nfz^\infectee\geq\max_{r\leq \infectee}\max\{t: \Infection_t^{r<\infectee+1}\in\InnovInfMarkedA{r<\infectee+1}[0,\nfz^{\infectee+1}\wedge t_r]\}\).

These considerations lead directly to the following definition:

:::{#def-no-fly-zone}
### No-fly zone
The _no-fly zone_ (\NFZ) on timeline \(\infectee\) is \([-\infty,\nfz^\infectee]\), 
defining \(\nfz^\infectee\) inductively: \(\nfz^\TotalRemovals =\max_{r\leq\TotalRemovals}\max\{t:\Removal_t^r\in \InnovRemMarkedR{r}\}\) 
(the latest of all in\activated removals), while
\[
\nfz^\infectee = 
\max_{r\leq \infectee}\max\{:t \Removal_t^r\in\InnovRemMarkedR{r}\}
\vee 
\max_{r\leq \infectee}\max\{t: \Infection_t^{r<\infectee+1}\in\InnovInfMarkedA{r<\infectee+1}[0,\nfz^{\infectee+1}\wedge t_r]\}\,,
\]  {#eq-nfz-boundary} 
for \(1{\leq}\infectee{<}\TotalRemovals\).
We write \(\overrightarrow\nfz = (\nfz^1, \nfz^2, \dots, \nfz^\TotalRemovals)\) for the entire \NFZ.
::: 



By construction the no-fly zone boundary \(\nfz^\infectee\) is (weakly) increasing in \(\infectee\):
the first maximum in Equation (-@eq-nfz-boundary), 
\(\max_{r\leq \infectee}\max\{t: \Removal_t^r\in\InnovRemMarkedR{r}\}\), is non-decreasing in \(\infectee\)
while the second is bounded above by \(\nfz^{\infectee+1}\). 
Note that if the \State \((\InnovRem,\InnovInf,I_{0-})\) satisfies the conditioning
then \(\nfz^\infectee\) equals \(-\infty\) for any timeline \(j\le I_{0-}\);
since for \(\infectee\le I_{0-}\) in Equation (-@eq-nfz-boundary) both the sets over which the maximum is taken must necessarily be empty; 
see the proof of @lem-portrait-inequalities below.



The second timeline function is called the _infection transmission path_ (\ITP): this is determined by the set of (\activated) infection incidents belonging to the \history of a conditioned epidemic, and is composed of the process-times \(\itp^\infectee\) at which timeline \(\infectee\) becomes infected.
The intuition here is that timeline \(\infectee >I_{0-}\) becomes infected at the time \(\itp^\infectee\)
of the earliest infection \(\Infection_t^{\infector<\infectee}\) which:
avoids the no-fly zone (\(t>\nfz^\infectee\));
occurs in the interval \([\itp^{\infectee-1}, t_\infector]\) during which timelines \(\infectee{-}1\) and \(\infector\) are both infectious;
and occurs before all _conditioned_ removals \(\InnovRemMarkedC{[\infectee:\TotalRemovals]}\) assigned to timeline \(\infectee\) or higher. 
(If this last point were not satisfied, there would be some conditioned removal assigned to a timeline which is not infectious at the removal time; the removal would consequently not be \activated, breaking the conditioning.)

Our ultimate aim is to perfectly sample from the joint distribuition of the \ITP and the number of initial infectives, \(I_{0-}\), 
conditioned on \activated removals occurring at \(t_1,\ldots,t_\TotalRemovals\).

:::{#def-infection-transmission-path}
### Infection transmission path
The _infection transmission path_ (\ITP) is composed of the process-times \(\itp^\infectee\) at which timeline \(\infectee\) becomes infected, and is defined inductively by
\[
\begin{aligned}
\itp^\infectee \quad=&\quad -\infty\,, &\text{ if \(1\le \infectee\le I_{0-}\),}  
\\ 
\itp^\infectee \quad=&\quad \min\bigsqcup_{\infector < \infectee} \InnovInfMarkedA{\infector<\infectee}
  [\itp^{\infectee{-}1}\vee \nfz^\infectee,\,\min\InnovRemMarkedC{[\infectee:\TotalRemovals]} \wedge t_\infector]\,,
& \text{ if \(I_{0-} < \infectee \le \TotalRemovals\).}
\end{aligned}
\] {#eq-itp-boundary}  
We write \(\overrightarrow\itp = (\itp^1, \itp^2, \dots, \itp^\TotalRemovals)\) for the entire \ITP.
:::

<!-- [SBC]: don't actually need reference to t_\infector in this definition, due to assumption above that there are no infections after removal time. Keeping it here for now, in case it's useful later on for monotonicity. -->

Note that the event \(\{\itp^\infectee=\infty\}\) will not arise for any \(\infectee\), since we have assumed the \State \((\InnovRem,\InnovInf,I_{0-})\) to yield an epidemic with exactly \(\TotalRemovals\) conditioned removals at times \(t_1,\ldots,t_\TotalRemovals\):
a proposal to either remove an infection, or to alter the value of \(I_{0-}\), in an epidemic satisfying this conditioning will not be allowed if this is a consequence.





The final timeline function that we require is named the _laziest feasible epidemic_ (\LFE). This is the slowest possible (in process-time) epidemic that can be created by deleting potential infections while preserving the conditioned removals (and avoiding the activation of any potential removals, as always). 
The rationale for the definition of \(\lfe^\infectee\) is that
this will be the latest infection \(\Infection_t^{\infector<\infectee}\) which: occurs before the time 
\(\lfe^{\infectee{+}1}\)
at which the laziest feasible epidemic reaches timeline \(\infectee{+}1\); occurs before the \(\infector^\text{th}\) removal time, \(t_\infector\); and occurs before all conditioned removals assigned to timeline \(\infectee\) or higher. 

:::{#def-laziest-feasible-epidemic}
### Laziest feasible epidemic
The _laziest feasible epidemic_ (\LFE) reaches timeline \(\infectee\)
at time \(\lfe^\infectee\), defined inductively by
setting \(\lfe^{\TotalRemovals+1}=t_\TotalRemovals\) and then defining
\[
\lfe^\infectee \quad=\quad \max\bigsqcup_{\infector < \infectee} \InnovInfMarkedA{\infector<\infectee}
  [0,\, \lfe^{\infectee{+}1} \wedge \min\InnovRemMarkedC{[\infectee:\TotalRemovals]} \wedge t_\infector]\,,
\quad 1\le \infectee\le \TotalRemovals \,.
\] {#eq-lfe-boundary}

We write \(\overrightarrow\lfe = (\lfe^1, \lfe^2, \dots, \lfe^\TotalRemovals)\) for the entire \LFE.
:::


<!-- Note that if timeline \(\infectee\) is conditioned to be removed at time  -->
<!-- \(t_\infectee\) for all \(\infectee\), then for each \(\infectee>R_{0-}+I_{0-}\) there must be _some_ potential infection -->
<!-- satisfying the conditions expressed in the supremum in Equation (-@eq-last-epidemic).  -->

<!-- ![No-fly zone (blue), infection transmission path (orange), and laziest feasible epidemic (dark) for this graphical representation.](fig-NFZ-LFE){#fig-NFZ-LFE fig-scap="\NFZ (TO BE REMOVED)"} -->


The three functions just introduced convey information about the essential structure of a conditioned epidemic; we gather them together, along with the vectors of in\activated and conditioned removals, and the number of initial infectives, to form the _epidemic portrait_.

:::{#def-epidemic-portrait}
### Epidemic portrait
Given a \State \((\InnovRem,\InnovInf,I_{0-})\), the corresponding _epidemic portrait_ is given by
\[
\Epidemic \quad=\quad (\overrightarrow\InnovRem_{\Removal}, \overrightarrow\nfz,  I_{0-}, \overrightarrow\itp, \overrightarrow\lfe, \overrightarrow\InnovRem_{\CRemoval}) \,.
\]
:::

Our final result of this section shows that the portrait corresponding to a conditioned epidemic satisfies some intuitive inequalities on each timeline.

:::{#lem-portrait-inequalities}
Let \((\InnovRem,\InnovInf,I_{0-})\) be a \State which yields an epidemic with \activated removals occurring precisely at times \(t_1{<\ldots<}t_\TotalRemovals\) in \([0,\Duration)\). The corresponding epidemic portrait satisfies the following inequalities on each timeline \(1\le \infectee \le \TotalRemovals\):
\[
\max \InnovRemMarkedR{[1:\infectee]} \le \nfz^\infectee
\;\le\; \itp^\infectee
\;\le\; \lfe^\infectee 
\;\le\; \min \InnovRemMarkedC{[\infectee:\TotalRemovals]}
\;\le\; t_\infectee \,.
\] {#eq-event-order}
:::

That is, the time at which timeline \(\infectee\) becomes infected
(\(\itp^\infectee\)) must lie outside of the no-fly zone (with boundary
\(\nfz^\infectee\)), and occur no later than the laziest feasible epidemic time
(\(\lfe^\infectee\)); this in turn must occur before the first
conditioned removal assigned to that timeline or one of a higher index 
(\(\min \InnovRemMarkedC{[\infectee:\TotalRemovals]}\)). 

:::{.proof}
For all timelines, the final inequality in (-@eq-event-order) is trivial (since \(t_\infectee \in \InnovRemMarkedC{[\infectee:\TotalRemovals]}\)), and the penultimate inequality follows from @def-laziest-feasible-epidemic. Similarly, the first inequality follows from 
<!--(-@eq-no-pot-removals-on-initial-infective) and -->
@def-no-fly-zone. We deal with the remaining inequalities (\( \nfz^\infectee \le \itp^\infectee \le \lfe^\infectee\)) by considering different values of \(\infectee\).

For \(\infectee\le I_{0-}\), @def-infection-transmission-path shows that \(\itp^\infectee = -\infty\), and it therefore suffices to show that \(\nfz^\infectee\) also equals \(-\infty\). This follows from Equation (-@eq-no-pot-removals-on-initial-infective) and the observation that the set 
\[
\bigsqcup_{\infector\le\infectee} \InnovInfMarkedA{\infector<\infectee+1}[0,\nfz^{\infectee+1}\wedge t_\infector]
\]
appearing in @def-no-fly-zone is empty. 
<!-- When \(\infectee\le R_{0-}\) this is guaranteed by @def-no-fly-zone; when \(R_{0-} <\infectee \le R_{0-}+I_{0-}\), the claim follows from Equation (-@eq-no-pot-removals-on-initial-infective) and the observation that the set 
\[
\bigsqcup_{\infector\le\infectee} \InnovInfMarkedA{\infector<\infectee+1}[0,\nfz^{\infectee+1}\wedge t_\infector]
\]
appearing in @def-no-fly-zone is empty. 
-->
For if not, it would contain a potential infection \(\Infection_t^{\infector<\infectee+1}\) with \(t\le\nfz^{\infectee+1}\), which would connect the \ITP to the \NFZ; such an infection is impossible under the conditioning (since it would necessarily lead to activation of a potential removal).

Finally, we consider a timeline \(I_{0-} <\infectee\). Here the inequality \( \nfz^\infectee \le \itp^\infectee\) follows from the second equation in @def-infection-transmission-path. For the one remaining inequality we proceed by induction, starting from \(\infectee = \TotalRemovals\). First observe that a conditioned epidemic must certainly satisfy \(\itp^{\TotalRemovals-1} \le \itp^{\TotalRemovals} \le t_\TotalRemovals\), since the infection path has to reach timeline \(\TotalRemovals\) before the final conditioned removal time. @def-no-fly-zone and @def-laziest-feasible-epidemic show that 
\(\nfz^\TotalRemovals = \max \InnovRemMarkedR{[1:\TotalRemovals]}\)
and 
\(\lfe^{\TotalRemovals+1} = t_\TotalRemovals \), 
and therefore 
\[
\itp^{\TotalRemovals-1} \vee \nfz^\TotalRemovals \le \lfe^{\TotalRemovals+1} \,.
\] {#eq-itp-lfe-order-help-1}  
Looking again at @def-infection-transmission-path and @def-laziest-feasible-epidemic, and bearing in mind that a conditioned epidemic must have both \ITP and \LFE activating all removals designated as "conditioned", this implies that the set 
\[
\bigsqcup_{\infector < \TotalRemovals} \InnovInfMarkedA{\infector<\TotalRemovals}
  [\itp^{\TotalRemovals{-}1}\vee \nfz^\TotalRemovals,\, \lfe^{\TotalRemovals{+}1} \wedge \min\InnovRemMarkedC{[\TotalRemovals:\TotalRemovals]} \wedge t_\infector]
\] {#eq-itp-lfe-order-help-2}   
is non-empty, and that \(\itp^\TotalRemovals\) and \(\lfe^\TotalRemovals\) will be the minimum and maximum (respectively) of this set. Thus \(\itp^\TotalRemovals \le \lfe^\TotalRemovals\). 

The functions \(\itp^\infectee\) and \(\nfz^\infectee\) are necessarily non-decreasing in \(\infectee\), so
\(\itp^{\TotalRemovals-2}\le \itp^\TotalRemovals\le \lfe^\TotalRemovals \) and 
\(\nfz^{\TotalRemovals-1} \le \nfz^\TotalRemovals \le \lfe^\TotalRemovals\). 
Thus Inequality (-@eq-itp-lfe-order-help-1) (and subsequent argument) holds with \(\TotalRemovals\) replaced by \(\TotalRemovals-1\). 
Repeating this argument, it follows that \(\itp^\infectee \le \lfe^\infectee\) for all \(\infectee\), as required.
:::




:::{.callout-important #imp-not-sure}
### Not for inclusion in submitted paper!
I'm not sure that the previous definitions were quite right for what we want to happen with time-0 infections. We were losing information as to whether there are any time-0 infections in \(\InnovInf\) where the infector and infectee both take values \(\le I_{0-}\): the \ITP looks the same whether or not such infections are present, but their presence will potentially affect perpetuation events. 

I think it would make sense to set \ITP and \LFE equal to \(-\infty\) for timelines \(\infectee\le I_{0-}\) **-- that change has now been implemented.**

Using that modification, here are some potential scenarios to bear in mind:

  - **Case 1**: \(\InnovRem_0 = \emptyset\), \(\InnovInf_0 = \emptyset\), \(I_{0-,0}=2\)
  - **Case 2**: \(\InnovRem_0 = \emptyset\), \(\InnovInf_0 = \{\Infection_0^{1<2}\}\), \(I_{0-,0}=2\)
  - **Case 3**: \(\InnovRem_0 = \emptyset\), \(\InnovInf_0 = \{\Infection_0^{1<2}\}\), \(I_{0-,0}=1\)
  
The corresponding epidemic portraits should have \(\nfz_0 = (-\infty,-\infty)\) in all three cases, and:

  - **Case 1**: \(\itp_0 = (-\infty,-\infty)\), \(\lfe_0 = (-\infty,-\infty)\)
  - **Case 2**: \(\itp_0 = (-\infty,-\infty)\), \(\lfe_0 = (-\infty,0)\)
  - **Case 3**: \(\itp_0 = (-\infty, 0)\), \(\lfe_0 = (-\infty,0)\)

Note that the \ITP and \LFE can now differentiate between the three cases (unlike the old definitions, in which they both would have equalled \((0,0)\) in all three cases).

Now suppose that we update, with \(\InnovRemMarked{*}_1 = \InnovInfMarkedA{*}_1 = \emptyset\), and \(I^*_1 = 1\). In Cases 1 and 2 we get \(\InnovInf_1 = \emptyset\), but in Case 3 the time-0 infection is perpetuated, and \(\InnovInf_1 = \{\Infection_0^{1<2}\}\). This should lead to the following portraits:

  - **Case 1**: \(\itp_1 = (-\infty,\infty)\), \(\lfe_1 = (-\infty,-\infty)\)
  - **Case 2**: \(\itp_1 = (-\infty,\infty)\), \(\lfe_1 = (-\infty,-\infty)\)
  - **Case 3**: \(\itp_1 = (-\infty, 0)\), \(\lfe_1 = (-\infty,0)\)

In particular, this means that \(I_{0-,1}=I_{0-,0}\) in all three cases. (The new proposed value is rejected in the first two, since conditioning is broken; and in Case 3 there is no change.)

:::


Evolution of the epidemic portrait {#sec:portrait-evolution}  {- .unlisted}
----------------------------------
Recall the construction in @thm-simplified-construction, which described the \algorithmictime evolution 
of a conditioned epidemic starting from initial \State
\((\InnovRem_0, \InnovInf_0, I_{0-,0})\)
and using the \ExtendedInnovation \((\InnovRemMarked{*}_1, \InnovInfMarkedA{*}_1, I^*_1, \InnovResampling^*_1)\) 
-- where \(\InnovResampling^*_1 = (m_1,m_2,\ldots)\) is a sequence of independent uniform draws from the set \(\{1,\ldots,\Population\}\) --
to arrive at \State 
\((\InnovRem_1, \InnovInf_1, I_{0-,1})\).
We now present a series of results which together permit a _direct_ 
construction of the corresponding epidemic portrait \(\Epidemic_1\) as a function of \(\Epidemic_0\) and the \ExtendedInnovation; in particular, these show that the sequence of portraits \((\Epidemic_n)_n\) is in fact a Markov chain.


:::{#lem-update-removals}
The sets of in\activated removals in \(\Epidemic_1\) are given by 
\[
\InnovRemMarked{\target}_{\Removal,1} = \{t\,:\, \Removal_t^\target \in \InnovRemMarked{*}_1 [0, \itp^\target_0) \} \,.
\]
Furthermore, the sets of conditioned removals in \(\Epidemic_1\) are determined by working through the removal times \(t_1,\dots,t_\TotalRemovals\) in order. For removal time \(t_\infectee\), we first locate the timeline \(\target\) to which it is allocated in \(\Epidemic_0\) (i.e. the value of \(\target\) such that \(t_\infectee \in \InnovRemMarked{\target}_{\CRemoval,0}\)). We then consider the draw \(m_\infectee\in \InnovResampling^*_1\) and proceed as follows:

  - if \(t_\infectee \in [\itp^{m_\infectee}_0 , t_{m_\infectee}] \), we allocate \(t_\infectee\) to timeline \(m_\infectee\) in \(\Epidemic_1\) (i.e. \(t_\infectee \in \InnovRemMarked{m_\infectee}_{\CRemoval,1}\));
  - otherwise, \(t_\infectee\) remains allocated to timeline \(\target\) in \(\Epidemic_1\) (i.e. \(t_\infectee \in \InnovRemMarked{\target}_{\CRemoval,1}\)).
:::


::: {.proof}
These follow directly from stages 1 and 2 of @thm-simplified-construction. In stage 1 all in\activated removals in \(\InnovRemMarked{\target}_{\Removal,0}\) are deleted, and replaced by exactly those potential removals in \(\InnovRemMarked{*}_{1}\) which have targets not lying in the infected region (and which therefore will not be \activated). In other words, only removals of the form \(\Removal_t^\target\) for which \(t<\itp^\target_0\) will be retained. In stage 2 we look to see whether timeline \(m_\infectee\) is infected at time \(t_\infectee\), i.e. whether \(\itp^{m_\infectee}_0 \le t_\infectee \le t_{m_\infectee} \): if so, the timeline to which the conditioned removal \(t_\infectee\) is assigned is updated to \(m_\infectee\); if not, the assignment remains unchanged.
:::

@fig-update-removals demonstrates these updates of in\activated and conditioned removals, beginning from the realisation in @fig-NFZ-LFE.

<!-- ![Demonstration removals update, beginning from realisation in @fig-NFZ-LFE. Inactivated removals (brown-edged disks) are replaced by a new set of inactivated removals conditioned to avoid infected region; some conditioned removals (purple-edged disks) are reassigned to different timelines (\(t_1,t_2\) to timeline 3, \(t_3\) to timeline 4).](fig-update-removals){#fig-update-removals fig-scap="Removals update (TO BE REMOVED)"} -->


We now turn our attention to the effect of updating infections, as in stage 3 of @thm-simplified-construction.
Recall that this is done by iterating over \(z\in\InnovInf_0 \sqcup \InnovInfMarkedA{*}_1\) in reverse \(\prec\) order, to arrive at the new set of potential infections, \(\InnovInf_1\). 
During this sweep we add new infections from \(\InnovInfMarkedA{*}_1\) to \(\InnovInf_1\) if doing so does not join the \ITP to the \NFZ (which would necessarily lead to the activation of a non-conditioned removal), and perpetuate an infection belonging to \(\InnovInf_0\) if removing it would cause the resulting \ITP not to activate every conditioned removal.

<!-- ![Demonstration of the update of infections, beginning from the realisation in @fig-update-removals.](fig-update-infections){#fig-update-infections fig-scap="Infections update (TO BE REMOVED)"} -->

@fig-update-infections demonstrates the effect of updating infections, 
beginning from the realisation in @fig-update-removals. The new set of potential infections in \(\InnovInfMarkedA{*}_1\) are shown with orange and dark grey edges; those with dark grey edges have been censored. In this realisation there are also three perpetuated infections, 
shown in dark green. Here follows a list of how infections have been updated in this realisation, 
moving through the diagram from right to left.

  1. The old infection \(\Infection_{11.0}^{4<5}\in\InnovInf_0\) is deleted as it is preceded by...
  2. ...the next \(\Infection_{10.0}^{4<5}\in\InnovInf_0\), which is _perpetuated_
	to ensure the two subsequent conditioned removals are \activated. (This means that \(\lfe_1^5 = 10.0\).)
  3. But a new \(\Infection_{9.0}^{4<5}\in \InnovInfMarkedA{*}_1\) is then introduced, which 
ends up as the time that the infection transmission path reaches timeline 5.
  4. Infection \(\Infection_{7.2}^{4<5}\in \InnovInfMarkedA{*}_1\) is _censored_, as it would infect the 
potential removal \(\Removal_{8.5}^{5}\).
  5. Then \(\Infection_{7.0}^{3<4} \in \InnovInfMarkedA{*}_1\) is introduced; it is the laziest feasible 
infection of timeline 4 (\(\lfe_1^4 = 7.0\)).
  6. Various old infections are now deleted, because they don't play essential parts in
the epidemic: in particular, the infections \(\Infection_{5.5}^{3<4}\) and \(\Infection_{5.0}^{2<4}\) can be deleted, becuase of the new infection \(\Infection_{7.0}^{3<4}\) which was just introduced.
  7. The new infection \(\Infection_{4.2}^{3<4}\in \InnovInfMarkedA{*}_1\) doesn't connect the \ITP to the \NFZ, and so doesn't risk infecting a removal _not_ designated as "conditioned", and can safely be introduced; it actually turns
out to form part of \(\itp_1\).
  8. Attention now turns to timeline 3. The old infection \(\Infection_{3.0}^{1<3}\in\InnovInf_0\)
is _perpetuated_ because at that stage it is the only possibility for infecting timeline 3 -- 
and in fact no earlier new infections will do so.
  9. Now the new infection \(\Infection_{2.2}^{4<5}\in \InnovInfMarkedA{*}_1\) will not have an effect
(it lies completetely within the no-fly zone), and so can safely be introduced.
  10. Old infection \(\Infection_{2.0}^{1<2}\in\InnovInf_0\) is _perpetuated_ to ensure timeline 2
is infected, though \(\Infection_{1.5}^{1<2}\in \InnovInfMarkedA{*}_1\) turns out to 
be the infection which causes \(\itp_1\) to reach timeline 2.
  11. Infection \(\Infection_{1.0}^{2<3}\in \InnovInfMarkedA{*}_1\) can also be safely introduced, and extends the 
no-fly zone \(\nfz_1\) since no earlier infection of timeline 2 can then be permitted.
  12. Finally, the new potential infection \(\Infection_{0.5}^{1<2}\in \InnovInfMarkedA{*}_1\) is _censored_, since it 
would connect the \ITP to \(\nfz_1\).



The next few results describe the evolution of the laziest feasible epidemic, 
no-fly zone and infection transmission path.

:::{#lem-update-lfe}
The laziest feasible epidemic in \(\Epidemic_1\), \(\overrightarrow\lfe_1\), can be determined as follows.
Set \(\lfe^{\TotalRemovals+1}_1 = t_\TotalRemovals\) and use the following recursion for \(1{\leq}\infectee{\leq}\TotalRemovals\):
\[
\lfe^\infectee_1  \quad=\quad
\itp^\infectee_0 \,\vee\,
\max\bigsqcup_{\infector < \infectee} \InnovInfMarkedB{*}{\infector<\infectee}
[0,\, \lfe^{\infectee{+}1}_1 \wedge \min\InnovRemMarked{[\infectee:\TotalRemovals]}_{\CRemoval,1} \wedge t_\infector]\,.
\] {#eq-update_laziest-feasible}
<!--(For timelines \(\infectee\le R_{0-}\), \(\lfe^{\infectee}_1 = -\infty\), by @def-laziest-feasible-epidemic.)--> 
:::

:::{.proof}
This follows from a similar argument to the rationale behind Equation (-@eq-lfe-boundary). 
Recall that when updating infections we work backwards through the process-time segment \([0, \Duration)\).
The laziest feasible epidemic must infect timeline \(\infectee\) 
before any conditioned removals currently assigned either to that timeline or 
to any timeline of greater index
(which is to say, no later than time \(\min\InnovRemMarked{[\infectee:\TotalRemovals]}_{\CRemoval,1}\)).
Moreover the laziest feasible epidemic must reach timeline \(\infectee\) 
no later than the time \(\lfe^{\infectee{+}1}_1\) at which 
the laziest feasible epidemic reaches the timeline above (indexed by \(\infectee{+}1\)). 
Finally, if the laziest feasible infection of timeline \(\infectee\)
is an infection from timeline \(\infector<\infectee\), then this must happen
before time \(t_\infector\) when timeline \(\infector\) is removed from the epidemic.

Consequently, given the value of \(\lfe^{\infectee{+}1}_1\), 
if the set \(\sqcup_{\infector<\infectee}\InnovInfMarkedB{*}{\infector<\infectee}\) contains at least one new potential infection incident of the form
\(\Infection_t^{\infector< \infectee}\), with \(t\) in the interval 
\[
(\itp^\infectee_0\,,\;\lfe^{\infectee{+}1}_1 \wedge  \min\InnovRemMarked{[\infectee:\TotalRemovals]}_{\CRemoval,1} \wedge t_\infector]\,,
\]
then \(\lfe^\infectee_1\) will be the maximum of these times. If not, then 
\(\lfe^\infectee_1 = \itp^\infectee_0\), either because of a perpetuated infection at process-time \(\itp^\infectee_0\), 
or because \(\infectee \le I_{0-,0}\) and \(\itp^\infectee_0 = -\infty\).
:::




:::{#lem-update-nfz}
The no-fly zone boundary in \(\Epidemic_1\) satisfies \(\nfz^\TotalRemovals_1 = \max \InnovRemMarked{[1:\TotalRemovals]}_{\Removal,1}\), and for \(\infectee < \TotalRemovals\):
\[
\nfz^\infectee_1 \quad=\quad 
  \max \InnovRemMarked{[1:\infectee]}_{\Removal,1} \vee 
  \max\bigsqcup_{\infector\le\infectee} \InnovInfMarkedB{*}{\infector<\infectee+1}_1
  [0,\,\itp^\infectee_0\wedge\nfz^{\infectee+1}_1 \wedge t_\infector]\,.
\] {#eq-update_no-fly_direct}
Furthermore, the inequality \(\nfz^\infectee_1 \le \itp^\infectee_0 \le \lfe^\infectee_1\) holds almost surely for all timelines \(\infectee\), with the first inequality being strict when \(\infectee > I_{0-,0}\). 
:::

:::{.proof}
The formula for \(\nfz^\TotalRemovals_1\) follows directly from @def-no-fly-zone. @lem-update-removals and @lem-update-lfe, along with the fact that the infection transmission path \(\itp_0^\infectee\) is weakly increasing in \(\infectee\), show that
\[ 
\nfz^\TotalRemovals_1 \quad =\quad
\max \InnovRemMarked{[1:\TotalRemovals]}_{\Removal,1} \quad <\quad \itp^\TotalRemovals_0 \quad \le\quad \lfe^\TotalRemovals_1 \,.
\]

We proceed by induction. Suppose that  \(\nfz^{\infectee+1}_1 <\itp^{\infectee+1}_0 \le \lfe^{\infectee+1}_1\) for some \(I_{0-,0} < \infectee<\TotalRemovals\).
Consideration of @def-no-fly-zone shows that Equation (-@eq-update_no-fly_direct) will follow if we can demonstrate that
\[
 \InnovInfMarkedA{\infector<\infectee+1}_1 [0,\nfz^{\infectee+1}_1]
 \quad =\quad
 \InnovInfMarkedB{*}{\infector<\infectee+1}_1
  [0,\,\itp^\infectee_0\wedge\nfz^{\infectee+1}_1 ] 
\]{#eq-update_no-fly_direct-equiv}
for all \(\infector\le \infectee\). 
Recall that the set 
\(\InnovInf_1 \subset \InnovInf_0 \sqcup \InnovInfMarkedA{*}_1\) 
is obtained by censoring any infection in \(\InnovInfMarkedA{*}_1\) which would cause the gap between the infection transmission path and the no-fly zone to be bridged, and also possibly perpetuating some infections belonging to the set 
\(\InnovInf_0\). If an infection of the form \(\Infection_t^{\infector<\infectee+1} \in \InnovInf_0\) is perpetuated during this update, it will by definition occur at process-time \(t=\lfe^{\infectee+1}_1\), i.e. the time at which the laziest feasible epidemic reaches timeline \(\infectee+1\). By our inductive assumption, this is strictly greater than \(\nfz^{\infectee+1}_1\), and so no perpetuated infection features in the set on the left-hand side of 
Equation (-@eq-update_no-fly_direct-equiv). This implies that
\[
\InnovInfMarkedA{\infector<\infectee+1}_1 [0,\nfz^{\infectee+1}_1]
 \quad \subseteq \quad
 \InnovInfMarkedB{*}{\infector<\infectee+1}_1
  [0,\nfz^{\infectee+1}_1] \,.
\]
Now consider the effect of censoring. 
The infections which are censored during this update are precisely those of the form 
\(\Infection_t^{\infector<\infectee+1} \in \InnovInfMarkedB{*}{\infector<\infectee+1}_1\) for which \(t\) belongs to the (possibly empty) process-time interval \([\itp^{\infectee}_0, \nfz^{\infectee+1}_1]\), since any such infection would immediately join the infection transmission path to the no-fly zone on timeline \(\infectee+1\), and would thereby break our conditioning. It follows that Equation (-@eq-update_no-fly_direct-equiv), and hence Equation (-@eq-update_no-fly_direct), holds for timeline \(\infectee\).

Finally, we recall once again from @lem-update-removals that \(\max \InnovRemMarked{[1:\infectee]}_{\Removal,1} < \itp^\infectee_0\). From equation (-@eq-update_no-fly_direct), @lem-update-lfe, and the fact that the Poisson process \(\InnovInfMarkedB{*}{\infector<\infectee+1}_1\) will almost surely not contain a potential infection at time \(t=\itp^\infectee_0\), we obtain:
\[
\nfz^\infectee_1  \quad < \quad \itp^\infectee_0 \quad\le \quad \lfe^\infectee_1 \,, \quad \text{a.s.}
\]
This shows that the required ordering holds on timeline \(\infectee\).

For timelines \(\infectee\le I_{0-,0}\), we saw in the proof of @lem-portrait-inequalities that \(\nfz^\infectee_1 = \itp^\infectee_0=-\infty\), and so the required inequality trivially holds.
:::



The two components of \(\Epidemic_1\) yet to be determined are the inital number of infectives \(I_{0-,1}\) and the infection transmission path, \(\overrightarrow\itp_1\). Recall from step 4 of @thm-simplified-construction that the former of these is the result of a rejection-sampling update. A new value \(I^*_1\) 
is generated from some proposal distribution with support \(\support(I^*)\): if the epidemic using this value has \activated removals precisely at times \(t_1<t_2<\ldots< t_\TotalRemovals\) then we set 
\(I_{0-,1} = I^*_1\); otherwise we set 
\(I_{0-,1} = I_{0-,0}\).
Rephrasing in terms of the epidemic portrait, the value \(I^*_1\) is rejected if and only if the corresponding infection transmission path \(\overrightarrow\itp_1\) does not activate exactly the required set of removals; equivalently, if and only if the ordering in Equation (-@eq-event-order) is broken on some timeline. 
In order to carry out this update, we therefore need to know how to calculate 
\(\overrightarrow\itp_1\) for any possible value of \(I^*_1\). 


:::{#lem-update-itp}
For each \(i_0\in \support(I^*)\), 
the infection trasmission path \(\overrightarrow\itp_1(i_0)\) corresponding to the \State \((\InnovRem_1,\InnovInf_1,I^*_1=i_0)\), 
i.e. with \(i_0\) initial infectives, is given as follows. 

For timelines \(\infectee\le i_0\): \(\itp^{\infectee}_1(i_0) = -\infty\). \
 <!-- \begin{equation}
\itp^{\infectee}_1(i_0) =  
\begin{cases}
    -\infty & \quad \text{if \(\nfz_1^\infectee = -\infty\)} \\
    \infty & \quad \text{otherwise.}
  \end{cases}
 
\label{eq-update-itp-direct1}
\end{equation}
 --> 
For timelines \(\infectee> i_0\):
\[
\itp^{\infectee}_1(i_0) =  
  \begin{cases}
    \min \bigsqcup_{\infector<\infectee} \InnovInfMarkedB{*}{\infector<\infectee}_1
      		  [\itp^{\infectee-1}_1(i_0) \vee \nfz^\infectee_1,\, \min\InnovRemMarked{[\infectee:\TotalRemovals]}_{\CRemoval,1} \wedge t_\infector] \\
      		  \hfill \text{if \(\lfe^\infectee_1 = -\infty\)} \\
    \min \bigsqcup_{\infector<\infectee} \InnovInfMarkedB{*}{\infector<\infectee}_1
        		  [\itp^{\infectee-1}_1(i_0) \vee \nfz^\infectee_1,\, \min\InnovRemMarked{[\infectee:\TotalRemovals]}_{\CRemoval,1} \wedge t_\infector]
        		\wedge \lfe^\infectee_1 \\
        		\hfill  \text{if \(\lfe^\infectee_1 \ge 0\).}
  \end{cases}
\] {#eq-update-itp-direct2}
:::


:::{.proof}
For \(\infectee\le i_0\) the result follows immediately from @def-infection-transmission-path.
For \(i_0{<}\infectee{\leq}\TotalRemovals\), @def-infection-transmission-path shows that the infection transmission path on timeline \(\infectee\) is given by
\[
\itp^\infectee_1(i_0) \quad=\quad \min\bigsqcup_{\infector < \infectee} \InnovInfMarkedA{\infector<\infectee}_1
  [\itp^{\infectee{-}1}_1(i_0) \vee \nfz^\infectee_1,\,\min\InnovRemMarked{[\infectee:\TotalRemovals]}_{\CRemoval,1} \wedge t_\infector]\,.
\]
We have already seen that \(\InnovInfMarkedA{\infector<\infectee}_1\) is obtained by censoring some potential infections belonging to \(\InnovInfMarkedB{*}{\infector<\infectee}_1\) and, in the event that \(\lfe^\infectee_1\ge 0\), possibly perpetuating an infection at time \(\lfe^\infectee_1\). However, only potential infections of the form \(\Infection_t^{\infector< \infectee}\) belonging to the (possibly empty) process-time interval \([\itp^{\infectee-1}_0,\,\nfz^\infectee_1]\) are censored (since these would connect the path \(\overrightarrow\itp_0\) to the new no-fly zone \(\overrightarrow\nfz_1\) on timeline \(\infectee\)); 
almost surely the Poisson process 
\(\InnovInfMarkedB{*}{\infector<\infectee}_1\) 
contains no such infections[^1] within the process-time interval
\([\itp^{\infectee-1}_1(i_0)\vee \nfz^\infectee_1,\, \min\InnovRemMarked{[\infectee:\TotalRemovals]}_{\CRemoval,1}\wedge t_\infector)\).
Thus the only possible difference on this time interval between the sets \(\InnovInfMarkedA{\infector<\infectee}_1\) and 
\(\InnovInfMarkedB{*}{\infector<\infectee}_1\) is the potential presence in the former of a perpetuated infection 
at time \(\lfe^\infectee_1\); the final term in Equation (-@eq-update-itp-direct2) accounts for this possibility.
:::
[^1]: Almost surely there will not be an infection \(\Infection_t^{\infector< \infectee}\) _exactly_ at time \(\nfz^\infectee_1\): @lem-update-nfz shows that \(\nfz^\infectee_1\) is a function of two Poisson processes which are independent of \(\InnovInfMarkedB{*}{\infector<\infectee}_1\).


By construction, the path \(\overrightarrow\itp_1(I_{0-,0})\) will satisfy the conditioning, and hence the portrait Inequalities (-@eq-event-order), since the acceptance/rejection decisions for each potential removal and infection during the update from \(\Epidemic_0\) to \(\Epidemic_1\) were each made to ensure that this infection path would maintain precisely the correct set of conditioned removal times. 
The next result describes the outcomes of proposing either an increase or decrease to the number of initial infectives during the update to \(\Epidemic_1\).
