:::{#cor-itp-monotonic-in-i0}
Consider \(i^-_0,i^+_0\in\support(I^*_1)\) satisfying \(i^-_0 < I_{0-,0} < i^+_0\). 
A proposal of \(I^*_1=i^+_0\) will be accepted in the update to \(\Epidemic_1\) if and only if \(\nfz^\infectee_1 = -\infty\) for all timelines \(j\le i^+_0\). 
Furthermore, attempting to decrease the number of initial infectives cannot yield an earlier infection transmission path: for every timeline \(\infectee\),
\[
	 \itp^\infectee_1(I_{0-,0}) \quad \le \quad 	\itp^\infectee_1(i^-_0) \,.
\] {#eq-itp-monotonic-in-i0}
:::

Note that Equation (-@eq-itp-monotonic-in-i0) includes the possibility that \(\itp^\infectee_1(i^-_0)=\infty\) for some \(\infectee\), in which case a proposal of \(I^*_1=i^-_0\) would necessarily be rejected. (This can happen if there is a timeline \(i^-_0<\infectee \le I_{0-,0}\) with \(\lfe^\infectee_1=-\infty\), but for which the set of infections over which the minimum is taken in Equation (-@eq-update-itp-direct2) is empty; that is, when there is no way for the infection path starting from \(i^-_0\) initial infectives to reach timeline \(\infectee\) before the conditioned removal time \(t_\infectee\).)

:::{.proof}
Suppose that there is a non-trivial no-fly zone on some timeline \(\infectee \le i^+_0\), i.e. that \(\nfz^\infectee_1 \ge 0\). By @def-infection-transmission-path, the transmission path with \(i^+_0\) initial infectives satisfies \(\itp^\infectee_1(i^+_0) = -\infty\), and thus the epidemic portrait Inequalities of (-@eq-event-order) are broken on timeline \(\infectee\): a proposal of \(I^*_1=i^+_0\) would therefore be rejected.

Conversely, suppose that \(\nfz^\infectee_1 = -\infty\) for all timelines \(j\le i^+_0\). 
We just need to check that the portrait inequalities 
\[
  \nfz^\infectee_1 \quad\le\quad \itp^\infectee_1(i^+_0) \quad\le\quad \lfe^\infectee_1
\]
are satisfied for all timelines \(\infectee > i^+_0\).

From Equation (-@eq-update-itp-direct2) it is immediate that \(\nfz^\infectee_1 \le \itp^\infectee_1(i^+_0)\), and moreover that
\(\itp^\infectee_1(i_0)\) is an increasing function of \(\itp^{\infectee-1}_1(i_0)\); induction shows that 
\(\itp^\infectee_1(i^+_0) \le \itp^\infectee_1(I_{0-,0})\) for all \(\infectee\). 
We have observed that \((\InnovRem_1,\InnovInf_1,I_{0-,0})\) satisfies the conditioning, by construction, and so \(\itp^\infectee_1(I_{0-,0}) \le \lfe^\infectee_1\) for all \(\infectee\). Thus the required inequalities are satisfied, meaning that a proposed value of \(I^*_1=i^+_0\) would be accepted.

It remains to prove the inequality in (-@eq-itp-monotonic-in-i0). 
Since \((\InnovRem_1,\InnovInf_1,I_{0-,0})\) satisfies the conditioning, we know that \(\itp^\infectee_1(I_{0-,0}) <\infty\) for each \(\infectee\), and
<!-- Decreasing the number of initial infectives could yield an epidemic which fails to actvate all conditioned removals, i.e. for which \(\itp^\infectee_1(i'_0) = \infty\) for some timeline \(\infectee\); in this case the claim is trivially true.  -->
\(\itp^\infectee_1(I_{0-,0}) = -\infty\) for timelines \(\infectee\le I_{0-,0}\) (@def-infection-transmission-path). For timelines \(\infectee > I_{0-,0}\) the claim holds by induction, once again using the observation that the expressions for \(\itp^\infectee_1(i_0)\) in @lem-update-itp are increasing functions of \(\itp^{\infectee-1}_1(i_0)\).
:::




Monotonicity {#sec-monotonicity}  {- .unlisted}
------------
We have just seen that the epidemic portrait
\[
\Epidemic_{n-1} = (\overrightarrow\InnovRem_{\Removal,n-1}, \overrightarrow\nfz_{n-1}, I_{0-,n-1}, \overrightarrow\itp_{n-1}, \overrightarrow\lfe_{n-1}, \overrightarrow\InnovRem_{\CRemoval,n-1})
\]
may be updated using the \ExtendedInnovation 
\((\InnovRemMarked{*}_n, \InnovInfMarkedA{*}_n, I^*_n, \InnovResampling^*_n)\),
to produce the portrait \(\Epidemic_n\) in four simple steps:

  1. **Removals:** construct \(\overrightarrow\InnovRem_{\Removal,n}\) and \(\overrightarrow\InnovRem_{\CRemoval,n}\) as functions of  \(\overrightarrow\InnovRem_{\CRemoval,n-1}\), \(\overrightarrow\itp_{n-1}\), \(\InnovRemMarked{*}_n\)
and \(\InnovResampling^*_n\) (@lem-update-removals).
  2. **Laziest feasible epidemic:** construct \(\overrightarrow\lfe_{n}\) as a function of \(\overrightarrow\InnovRem_{\CRemoval,n}\), \(\overrightarrow\itp_{n-1}\) and \(\InnovInfMarkedA{*}_n\) (@lem-update-lfe).
  3. **No-fly zone:** construct \(\overrightarrow\nfz_{n}\) as a function of \(\overrightarrow\itp_{n-1}\), \(\overrightarrow\InnovRem_{\Removal,n}\) and \(\InnovInfMarkedA{*}_n\) (@lem-update-nfz). 
  4. **Infection transmission path:** construct \(\overrightarrow\itp_{n}\) and \(I_{0-,n}\) as a function of \(\overrightarrow\InnovRem_{\CRemoval,n}\),  \(\overrightarrow\nfz_{n}\), \(\overrightarrow\lfe_{n}\), \(\InnovInfMarkedA{*}_n\), 
  \(I_{0-,n-1}\) and \(I^*_n\) (@lem-update-itp). 


However, further consideration of this construction shows that, of all the information contained in \(\Epidemic_{n-1}\), only the values of 
\(I_{0-,n-1}\),  \(\overrightarrow\itp_{n-1}\) and \(\overrightarrow\InnovRem_{\CRemoval,n-1}\) are used in the update to \(\Epidemic_n\). 
This implies that the _epidemic projection_ 
\[
\ProjEpi_n = (I_{0-,n},  \overrightarrow\itp_{n}, \overrightarrow\InnovRem_{\CRemoval,n}) \,,
\]
which tracks only the number of initial infectives, the infection transmission path, and the allocation of conditioned removals to timelines, is a discrete-time Markov chain. Its state-space is 
\[\mathcal{X} = \support(I^*) \times [-\infty,T]^\TotalRemovals \times \mathcal{P}_\TotalRemovals \,,\]
where \(\mathcal{P}_\TotalRemovals\) denotes the set of ordered length-\(\TotalRemovals\) partitions of the set \(\{1,\dots,\TotalRemovals\}\). In this section we shall explore monotonicity of this chain with respect to a certain partial order, and then exploit this monotonicity to produce a CFTP algorithm to sample from the stationary distribution of \(\ProjEpi\).

:::{#def-epidemic-ordering}
### Partial order for epidemic projections
Consider two projections of conditioned epidemics \(\slower{\ProjEpi}_n\) and \(\faster{\ProjEpi}_n\). 
Write \(\slower{\ProjEpi}_n \trianglelefteq \faster{\ProjEpi}_n\) if and only if 
the following three relations hold:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\slower{I}_{0-,n}\quad &\le \quad \faster{I}_{0-,n} \,; & \\
\slower{\itp}^\infectee_{n}\quad &\ge \quad \widehat{\itp}^\infectee_{n} &\quad \text{for all timelines \(\infectee=1,\dots,\TotalRemovals\);} \\
\slower{\Pi}^{\textup{rem},[\infectee:\TotalRemovals]}_{\CRemoval,n} \quad &\subseteq \quad 
\faster{\Pi}^{\textup{rem},[\infectee:\TotalRemovals]}_{\CRemoval,n} &\quad \text{for all timelines \(\infectee=1,\dots,\TotalRemovals\).}
\end{aligned}
\]
:::


The intuition here is that \(\faster{\ProjEpi}_n\)
describes an epidemic that spreads through the population _no slower_ than \(\slower{\ProjEpi}_n\).
The \(I_{0-}\) and \ITP inequalities in @def-epidemic-ordering ensure that  \(\faster{\ProjEpi}_n\) has at least as many initial infectives as \(\slower{\ProjEpi}_n\), as well as an earlier transmission path  (and so the period of time for which each timeline is infected is at least as long in \(\faster{\ProjEpi}_n\) as in \(\slower{\ProjEpi}_n\)). Similarly, the final requirement forces each conditioned removal to be assigned to a timeline in \(\faster{\ProjEpi}_n\) with index at least as great as in \(\slower{\ProjEpi}_n\).
(Recall that the timeline to which a conditioned removal \(t_\infectee\) is assigned must be infected before time \(t_\infectee\),
and so assigning it to a higher timeline can only lead to an earlier infection transmission path.)


This partial ordering admits two extremal states, which we shall refer to as the "fastest" and "slowest" projections, and denote by \(\ProjEpi\fastest\) and \(\ProjEpi\slowest\), respectively. These extremal states have the earliest / latest possible transmission paths, given the pattern of conditioned removals, and any projection  \(\ProjEpi\) of a conditioned epidemic will satisfy \(\ProjEpi\slowest \trianglelefteq \ProjEpi \trianglelefteq \ProjEpi\fastest\). They are defined as follows, and were illustrated in @fig-fastest-slowest for the case when \(I^*\equiv 1\).

  - **Fastest epidemic:**
  \( \ProjEpi\fastest = (I_{0-}^\textup{fastest}, \overrightarrow\itp\fastest, \overrightarrow\InnovRemMarkedC{\textup{fastest}})\), where:

      - \(I_{0-}^\textup{fastest} = \max\support(I^*) \);
      
      - \(\overrightarrow\itp\fastest\) is given by
      \[
      \itp\fastest[,\infectee] = \begin{cases}
      -\infty \quad &\quad 1 \le \infectee\le I_{0-}^\textup{fastest} \\
      0 \quad & \quad I_{0-}^\textup{fastest} < \infectee \le\TotalRemovals \,;
      \end{cases}
      \]
      
      - \(\InnovRemMarkedC{\textup{fastest}, \TotalRemovals} = \{t_1,t_2,\ldots,t_\TotalRemovals\}\), and \(\InnovRemMarkedC{\textup{fastest}, \infectee} = \emptyset\) for all \(\infectee<\TotalRemovals\)  
      (i.e. all conditioned removals are assigned to timeline \(\TotalRemovals\)).
     
  Note that in the event that \(\max\support(I^*) < \TotalRemovals\), \( \ProjEpi\fastest\) is realisable as the projection of an epidemic \State with \(I_{0-}^\textup{fastest}\) initial infectives and a set of time-0 infections which lead to all timelines being infected instantaneously at time 0, as in @fig-fastest.


  - **Slowest epidemic:** 
  \(\ProjEpi\slowest = (I_{0-}^\textup{slowest}, \overrightarrow\itp\slowest, \overrightarrow\InnovRemMarkedC{\textup{slowest}})\), where:
    
      - \(I_{0-}^\textup{slowest} = \min\support(I^*) \);
      
      - the infection path \(\overrightarrow\itp\slowest\) reaches timeline \(\infectee\) at the last possible moment, just as timeline \(\infectee{-}1\) is removed at time \(t_{\infectee-1}\):
      \[
      \itp\slowest[,\infectee] = \begin{cases}
      -\infty \quad &\quad 1 \le \infectee\le I_{0-}^\textup{slowest} \\
      t_{\infectee-1} \quad & \quad I_{0-}^\textup{slowest} < \infectee \le\TotalRemovals \,;
      \end{cases}
      \]
    
      - \(\InnovRemMarkedC{\textup{fastest}, \infectee} = \{t_{\infectee}\}\) for \(1\le \infectee \le \TotalRemovals\) 
      (i.e. exactly one conditioned removal is assigned to each timeline).


:::{#thm-update-preserve-ordering}
Suppose that two projected epidemics satisfy \(\slower{\ProjEpi}_{n-1} \trianglelefteq \faster{\ProjEpi}_{n-1}\) for some \(n\in\Integers\). After updating both using the (common) \ExtendedInnovation \((\InnovRemMarked{*}_n, \InnovInfMarkedA{*}_n, I^*_n, \InnovResampling^*_n)\), this ordering is preserved: \(\slower{\ProjEpi}_{n} \trianglelefteq \faster{\ProjEpi}_{n}\).
:::

:::{.proof}
\(\ProjEpi_n\) is obtained as a projection of the epidemic \(\Epidemic_n\). 
Given \(\slower{\ProjEpi}_{n-1}  \trianglelefteq \faster{\ProjEpi}_{n-1}\), we construct \(\slower{\ProjEpi}_{n}\) and \(\faster{\ProjEpi}_{n}\) by considering the effect of updating removals and then infections, following the four steps identified at the start of this section.

**1. Removals.** 
Recall the two stages of updating removals as described in @lem-update-removals. For potential removals we 
  obtain:
  \[
  \begin{aligned}
  \faster{\Pi}^{\text{rem},\infectee}_{\Removal,n} \quad &= \quad  \{t\,:\, \Removal_t^\infectee \in \InnovRemMarked{*}_n [0, \widehat{\itp}^\infectee_{n-1}) \} \\
  &\subseteq \quad \{t\,:\, \Removal_t^\infectee \in \InnovRemMarked{*}_n [0, \itp^\infectee_{n-1}) \} \\
  &= \quad  \slower{\InnovRemMarked{\infectee}}_{\Removal,n}  \,.
  \end{aligned}
  \] {#eq-removals_order}  
For conditioned removals, the ordering at time \(n-1\) ensures that
  \[ 
  \slower{\Pi}^{\textup{rem},[\infectee:\TotalRemovals]}_{\CRemoval,{n-1}} \quad \subseteq \quad 
\faster{\Pi}^{\textup{rem},[\infectee:\TotalRemovals]}_{\CRemoval,{n-1}}\,.
  \]

The reassignment to timelines at time \(n\) of conditioned removal times follows an acceptance/rejection procedure, with the proposed new timeline \(m_\infectee\) for removal time \(t_\infectee\) being determined by the innovation \(\InnovResampling^*_n\); furthermore, the rejection rule in @lem-update-removals is monotonic in \(\slower{\itp}^{m_\infectee}_{n-1} \ge \widehat{\itp}^{m_\infectee}_{n-1}\). This implies that
\[
  \slower{\Pi}^{\textup{rem},[\infectee:\TotalRemovals]}_{\CRemoval,{n}} \quad \subseteq \quad 
\faster{\Pi}^{\textup{rem},[\infectee:\TotalRemovals]}_{\CRemoval,{n}}\,,
\] {#eq-conditioned-ordering-after-update}  
as required.

**2. Laziest feasible epidemic.**  
It is immediate from @lem-update-lfe that, given \(\InnovInfMarkedA{*}_n\), the laziest feasible epidemic \(\lfe^\infectee_n\) is increasing in both \(\itp^\infectee_{n-1}\) and \(\min\slower{\Pi}^{\textup{rem},[\infectee:\TotalRemovals]}_{\CRemoval,{n}}\). It follows from the assumption that \(\slower{\ProjEpi}_{n-1} \trianglelefteq \faster{\ProjEpi}_{n-1}\), combined with (-@eq-conditioned-ordering-after-update), that \(\slower{\lfe}^\infectee_n\ge \widehat{\lfe}^\infectee_n\).

**3: No-fly zone.** 
In (-@eq-removals_order) we established that 
\( \faster{\Pi}^{\text{rem},\infectee}_{\Removal,n} \subseteq \slower{\InnovRemMarked{\infectee}}_{\Removal,n}\), 
and the assumption that \(\slower{\ProjEpi}_{n-1} \trianglelefteq \faster{\ProjEpi}_{n-1}\) tells us that \(\slower{\itp}^\infectee_{n-1} \ge \widehat{\itp}^\infectee_{n-1}\). From @lem-update-nfz we see that \(\nfz^\infectee_n\) is increasing in \(\max \InnovRemMarked{[1:\infectee]}_{\Removal,n} \) and \(\itp^\infectee_{n-1}\), thus \(\slower{\nfz}^\infectee_n\ge \widehat{\nfz}^\infectee_n\).

**4. Infection transmission path.** 
The ordering at time \(n-1\) tells us that \(\slower{I}_{0-,n-1}\le \faster{I}_{0-,n-1}\). We first of all need to examine whether or not the proposed value \(I^*_n\) is accepted/rejected in the updates of the two processes at time \(n\). There are two cases which could potentially break monotonicity, and which therefore need to be ruled out:

  1. \(I^*_n < \slower{I}_{0-,n-1}\)
  , with \(I^*_n\) being _accepted_ in the update to \(\faster{\ProjEpi}_n\) but _rejected_ in the update to \(\slower{\ProjEpi}_n\).

  2. \(\faster{I}_{0-,n-1} < I^*_n \)
  , with \(I^*_n\) being _rejected_ in the update to \(\faster{\ProjEpi}_n\) but _accepted_ in the update to \(\slower{\ProjEpi}_n\).
  
In both cases we shall argue by contradiction. Recall that the proposed value is rejected if and only if the resulting epidemic portrait inequalities of @lem-portrait-inequalities are broken on some timeline; i.e. 
\(I^*_n\) is rejected in the update to \(\slower{\ProjEpi}_n\) if 
\(\slower{\itp}^\infectee_n(I^*_n) \notin [\slower{\nfz}^\infectee_n,\slower{\lfe}^\infectee_n]\)
for some \(\infectee\), and similarly for \(\faster{\ProjEpi}_n\). 

For Case 1, we remarked following @lem-update-itp that, by construction, the updated infection path will satisfy the conditioning if we do not change the initial number of infectives: \(\slower{\nfz}^\infectee_n \le \slower{\itp}^\infectee_n(I_{0-,n-1}) \le \slower{\lfe}^\infectee_n\). Furthermore, @cor-itp-monotonic-in-i0 shows that decreasing the number of initial infectives can only possibly delay the infection path: \(\slower{\itp}^\infectee_n(I^*_n) \ge \slower{\itp}^\infectee_n(I_{0-,n-1})\). 
Combining these observations shows that the only way in which the proposed \(I^*_n\) value can be rejected in \(\slower{\ProjEpi}_n\) is if there is a timeline \(\infectee\) for which 
\[
\slower{\lfe}^\infectee_n \quad<\quad \slower{\itp}^\infectee_n(I^*_n)\,.
\] {#eq-I0-monotonicity1}

Any timeline \(\infectee\le I^*_n\) satisfies \(\infectee\le I_{0-,n-1}\): 
this means that \(\slower{\itp}^\infectee_n(I_{0-,n-1}) = \slower{\nfz}^\infectee_n = -\infty\) (since using the previous number of initial infectives cannot break the ordering in (-@eq-event-order)). 
The first part of @lem-update-itp then implies that \(\slower{\itp}^\infectee_n(I^*_n) = -\infty\), 
and so (-@eq-I0-monotonicity1) cannot hold for any timeline \(\infectee\le I^*_n\). 

Suppose instead that \(\infectee > I^*_n\). By (-@eq-update-itp-direct2), if \(\slower{\lfe}^\infectee_n\) is non-negative, the infection transmission path with 
\(I^*_n\) initial infectives will certainly satisfy 
\(\slower{\itp}^\infectee_n(I^*_n) \le \slower{\lfe}^\infectee_n\). 
However, if \(\slower{\lfe}^\infectee_n = -\infty\) then Step 2 above shows that \(\widehat{\lfe}^\infectee_n = -\infty\); since we are assuming that the update to 
\(I^*_n\) is accepted in \(\faster{\ProjEpi}_n\), this forces
\(\widehat{\itp}^\infectee_n(I^*_n) =-\infty\) in order for the portrait inequalities to hold; but then @lem-update-itp shows that this is only possible if timeline \(\infectee\) satisfies 
\(\infectee \le I^*_n\), which is a contradiction. This rules out Case 1.

For Case 2, observe from @cor-itp-monotonic-in-i0 that \(I^*_n > \slower{I}_{0-,n-1}\) 
being accepted in the update to \(\slower{\ProjEpi}_n\) implies that 
\(\slower{\nfz}^\infectee_1 = -\infty\) for all \(\infectee\le I^*_n\). 
Step 3 above then implies that \(\widehat{\nfz}^\infectee_1 = -\infty\) for all \(\infectee\le I^*_n\), and a second use of @cor-itp-monotonic-in-i0 shows that 
\(I^*_n > \faster{I}_{0-,n-1}\) would also be accepted in the update to \(\faster{\ProjEpi}_n\). Thus Case 2 cannot occur, and we conclude that \(\slower{I}_{0-,n}\le \faster{I}_{0-,n}\).

<!-- For Case 2, @lem-update-nfz and @cor-itp-monotonic-in-i0 now show that rejection of \(I^*_n\) in the update to \(\faster{\ProjEpi}_n\) can only occur if there is a timeline \(\infectee\) with -->
<!-- \begin{equation} -->
<!-- \widehat{\itp}^\infectee_n(I^*_n) < \widehat{\nfz}^\infectee_n \,. -->
<!-- \label{eq-I_{0-}-monotonicity2} -->
<!-- \end{equation} -->
<!-- @lem-update-itp once again implies that this would force \(\infectee \le R_{0-}+I^*_n\), in which case \(\widehat{\itp}^\infectee_n(I^*_n) = -\infty\). However, in order for \(I^*_n\) to be accepted in the update to \(\slower{\ProjEpi}_n\), it must be the case that \(\slower{\nfz}^\infectee_n = -\infty\), since otherwise  -->
<!-- \(I^*_n > i_{0,n}^{\max}\). But then by Step 3 above it follows that \(\widehat{\nfz}^\infectee_n = -\infty\), which contradicts (-@eq-I_{0-)-monotonicity2}; this rules out Case 2. -->
<!-- It follows that \(\slower{I}_{0,n}\le \faster{I}_{0,n}\). -->

Finally, we need to demonstrate that for all timelines \(\infectee\),
\[
  \widehat{\itp}^\infectee_n(\faster{I}_{0-,n}) \quad\le\quad \slower{\itp}^\infectee_n(\slower{I}_{0-,n})\,.
\]
Observe from @lem-update-itp that \(\widehat{\itp}^\infectee_n(\faster{I}_{0-,n}) = -\infty\) for \(\infectee \le \faster{I}_{0-,n}\) and for any \(\infectee\) for which \(\widehat{\lfe}^\infectee_n = -\infty\) (since \(\faster{\ProjEpi}_n\) will necessarily satisfy the portrait inequalities). For all other values of \(\infectee\), the required inequality follows
by induction, using the fact that the transmission path in (-@eq-update-itp-direct2) is an increasing function of \(\nfz^\infectee_n\), \(\min\Pi^{\textup{rem},[\infectee:\TotalRemovals]}_{\CRemoval,{n}}\) and \(\lfe^\infectee_n\), along with the results of Steps 1--3 above.

Taken together, the results of Steps 1--4 show that 
\(\slower{\ProjEpi}_{n} \trianglelefteq \faster{\ProjEpi}_{n}\),
as required.
:::


:::{.callout-note #nte-note-about-monotonicity}
### Conjectural note
I guess that effectively the same proof should show that monotonicity is still maintained if \(\slower{\ProjEpi}_{n-1}\) is updated using innovation \((\InnovRemMarked{*}_n, \InnovInfMarkedA{*}_n, \slower{I}^*_n, \InnovResampling^*_n)\)
and \(\faster{\ProjEpi}_{n-1}\) updated using innovation \((\InnovRemMarked{*}_n, \InnovInfMarkedA{*}_n, \faster{I}^*_n, \InnovResampling^*_n)\), 
as long as 

  - \(\slower{I}^*_n \le \faster{I}^*_n \)
  - and we never have \(\slower{I}^*_n < \faster{I}^*_n < \slower{I}_{0-,n-1}\) or
  \(\faster{I}_{0-,n-1} < \slower{I}^*_n < \faster{I}^*_n \) (since these could potentially lead to a bad reject/accept outcome).

This means that something like a RWMH sampler for updating \(I_{0-}\) should be ok.
:::


CFTP for the epidemic projection  {- .unlisted}
--------------------------------
The existence of two extremal states, and the observation that our partial order is preserved by the evolution in \algorithmictime of our coupled Markov chains, nicely sets the scene for an implementation of a CFTP algorithm for sampling from the equilibrium distribution of an epidemic conditioned to infect all individuals before the conditioned removal times. Starting from time \(-n<0\) for some positive integer \(n\), evolve two copies of the process \(\slower\ProjEpi\) and \(\faster\ProjEpi\) beginning at states \(\slower\ProjEpi_{-n} = \ProjEpi\slowest\) and \(\faster\ProjEpi_{-n} = \ProjEpi\fastest\), and using the same \ExtendedInnovation sequence. The monotonicity arguments laid out above ensure that \(\slower\ProjEpi_m \trianglelefteq \faster\ProjEpi_m\) for \(m{=}-(n-1){,\dots,}0\). If \(\slower\ProjEpi_0 = \faster\ProjEpi_0\) then return their common value as a draw from equilibrium; if not, then set \(n\leftarrow 2n\) and repeat, reusing the previously generated \ExtendedInnovation at any step \(m\ge -n\). 

The use of 'binary backoff' (doubling the value of \(n\) any time that coalescence has not been achieved, and a new iteration of the algorithm is begun) is an efficient approach to finding the backwards coalescence time of the two bounding chains, and is commonly used in CFTP algorithms. Note that if during some iteration of the algorithm we begin at time \(-2n\) with \((\slower\ProjEpi_{-2n},\faster\ProjEpi_{-2n}) = (\ProjEpi\slowest,\ProjEpi\fastest)\), then at time \(-n\) these realisations will of course satisfy 
\[ 
\ProjEpi\slowest \quad\trianglelefteq\quad \slower\ProjEpi_{-n}\quad \trianglelefteq \quad \faster\ProjEpi_{-n}\quad  \trianglelefteq \quad \ProjEpi\fastest \,.
\]
Reuse of the innovations \(m\ge -n\) will ensure that \(\slower\ProjEpi\) and \(\faster\ProjEpi\) will be 'sandwiched' over this period between chains started from the extremal states at time \(-n\).

Note that once \(\slower{\ProjEpi}_{n-1} = \faster{\ProjEpi}_{n-1}\), we will necessarily have agreement of the _entire_ epidemic portraits at the next update: \(\slower{\Epidemic}_n = \widehat{\Epidemic}_n\). (This can be seen by looking at the four steps of updating the epidemic portrait chain, as outlined at the start of the previous section on monotonicity.)


:::{#thm-CFTP-works}
The coalescence time of the \CFTP algorithm sketched above is almost surely finite (and thus the algorithm samples from the equilibrium distribution of (the projection of) an \SIR epidemic conditioned upon the conditioned removal times).
:::

In the language of stochastic stability, the proof of @thm-CFTP-works shows that the entire state-space \(\mathcal{X}\) is a _small set of lag 2_; for any given state \(\ProjEpi_{n-1}=x\), with probability \(\gamma\eps>0\) (to be defined below) the value of \(\ProjEpi_{n+1}\) can be drawn from a distribution on \(\mathcal{X}\) which is independent of \(x\). This is equivalent to the chain being uniformly ergodic (@MeynTweedie-1993), and also to the existence of a CFTP algorithm for sampling from its equilibrium distribution (@FossTweedie-1998).

:::{.proof}
We shall work under the assumption that \(0<t_1\), i.e. that the first conditioned removal time is strictly positive; the case when \(t_1=0\) is very similar. 

Fix some constant \(\delta \in (0,t_1)\). Given \(\delta\), we shall identify a set \(F_\delta \subset \mathcal{X}\) of epidemic projections which satisfies the following three properties:

  1. there exists \(\gamma>0\) such that
      \[ \inf_{x\in\mathcal{X}} \Prob{\ProjEpi_n\in F_\delta\,|\, \ProjEpi_{n-1}=x} \quad \ge \quad \gamma\,; \]
  
  2. \(F_\delta\) is at the 'top' of the state-space, meaning that
	   \(\slower{\ProjEpi}_n \trianglelefteq \faster{\ProjEpi}_n\) and 
	   \(\slower{\ProjEpi}_n \in F_\delta\) then \(\faster{\ProjEpi}_n \in F_\delta\);		
	   
  3. there exists \(\eps>0\) such that  
      \[ 
      \inf_{x,\faster{x}\, \in\, F_\delta} \Prob{\slower{\ProjEpi}_{n+1} =
      \faster{\ProjEpi}_{n+1} \,|\, \slower{\ProjEpi}_n = x \trianglelefteq \faster{x} = \faster{\ProjEpi}_n} 
      \quad\ge\quad
      \eps \,.
      \]

Item 1 shows that the time taken for a chain \(\ProjEpi\) started from the bottom state \(\ProjEpi\slowest\) to enter the set \(F_\delta\) is dominated by a geometric random variable with mean \(1/\gamma\); Items 2 and 3 show that whenever this event occurs, the chain \(\faster\ProjEpi\) -- started from the top state \(\ProjEpi\fastest\) and coupled to lie above \(\slower\ProjEpi\) -- will also lie within \(F_\delta\), and with probability at least \(\eps>0\) the two projections will coalesce at the next time point. We deduce that their coalescence time is almost surely finite. 

It remains to identify a set \(F_\delta\) for which Items 1-3 above are satisfied. Let \(F_\delta\) be the set of epidemics for which the epidemic \trajectory reaches the highest timeline \(\TotalRemovals\) (so all individuals are infected) by time \(\delta\): 
<!-- (see Figure~\ref{fig:small_set}): -->
\[
	F_\delta \quad=\quad
	\{ (I_{0-},  \overrightarrow\itp, \overrightarrow\InnovRem_{\CRemoval} )\in \mathcal{X} \,:\, \itp^\TotalRemovals \le \delta\} \,.
\]
 This clearly satisfies Item 2, since if \(\slower{\ProjEpi}_n \trianglelefteq \faster{\ProjEpi}_n\) and \(\slower{\itp}^\TotalRemovals_n \le \delta\), then \(\widehat{\itp}^\TotalRemovals_n \le \delta\) follows from @def-epidemic-ordering, and thus \(\faster{\ProjEpi}_n\in F_\delta\).

For Item 1 consider, for \(x = (I_{0-,n-1},  \overrightarrow\itp_{n-1}, \overrightarrow\InnovRem_{\CRemoval,n-1} ) \),
\[
\begin{aligned}
	\Prob{\ProjEpi_n \in F_\delta\,|\, \ProjEpi_{n-1}=x} \quad&\ge\quad 
	\Prob{\ProjEpi_n\in F_\delta\,|\, \InnovRem_{\Removal,n} =\emptyset,\, \ProjEpi_{n-1}=x}\Prob{\InnovRem_{\Removal,n} =\emptyset\,|\, \ProjEpi_{n-1}=x}   \\
	&=
	\quad \Prob{\ProjEpi_n\in F_\delta\,|\, \InnovRem_{\Removal,n}=\emptyset,\, \ProjEpi_{n-1}=x} 
	\prod_{\infectee> I_{0-,n-1}} \exp(-\beta\, \itp^\infectee_{n-1} ) \\
	&\ge
	\quad \Prob{\ProjEpi_n\in F_\delta\,|\, \InnovRem_{\Removal,n}=\emptyset,\, \ProjEpi_{n-1}=x} \exp(-\beta\sum_{\infectee=1}^{\TotalRemovals} t_\infectee) \,,
\end{aligned}
\] {#eq-F_delta_bound}  
where in this final step we have bounded \(\Prob{\InnovRem_{\Removal,n}=\emptyset\,|\, \ProjEpi_{n-1}=x} \) uniformly over \(x\in \mathcal{X}\) by the probability that the Poisson process \(\InnovRem_{\Removal,n}\) puts no potential removals on any timeline \(\infectee\) before the corresponding conditioned removal time \(t_\infectee\). 

Thanks to the monotonicity in \(I_{0-}\) (@cor-itp-monotonic-in-i0), the remaining probability in (-@eq-F_delta_bound) may now be bounded below, uniformly for all values of \(\ProjEpi_{n-1}\), by the probability that the Poisson process \(\InnovInfMarkedA{*}_n\) contains a set of potential infections which would lead to an infection transmission path starting from \(I_{0-}=1\) reaching level \(\TotalRemovals\) by time \(\delta\), given that there are no in\activated removals to avoid (since we have conditioned on the event that \(\InnovRem_{\Removal,n}=\emptyset\)).

One possible bound is given by dividing the interval \([0,\delta]\) into subintervals of length \(\delta/(\TotalRemovals-1)\), and requiring there to be at least one infection incident which would lead to the transmission path advancing from timeline \(\infector\) to \(\infector+1\) during the \(\infector^\text{th}\) interval, for \(\infector = 1,\dots,\TotalRemovals-1\): this gives a lower bound of 
	\[ 
		\Prob{\ProjEpi_n\in F_\delta\,|\, \InnovRem_{\Removal,n}=\emptyset,\, \ProjEpi_{n-1}=x} \quad\ge\quad \prod_{\infector=1}^{\TotalRemovals-1}(1- e^{-\infector(\Population-\infector)\alpha\delta/(\TotalRemovals-1)})\,.
	\]
Putting this bound into (-@eq-F_delta_bound) demonstrates that \(F_\delta\) satisfies the requirement of Item 1.

Finally, consider Item 3. Let \(A_{n+1}\) denote the event that the Poisson process \(\InnovInfMarkedA{*}_{n+1}[\delta,t_1)\) contains a set of potential infections which, in the absence of any removal events, would cause an infection transmission path starting from timeline 1 _at process-time \(\delta\)_ to reach timeline \(\TotalRemovals\) before process-time \(t_1\). The events \(\{A_n\}\) are i.i.d., have positive probability, and \(A_{n+1}\) is independent of both \(\slower{\ProjEpi}_{n}\) and \(\faster{\ProjEpi}_{n}\). 
Let \(I^{*,\max} = \max\{\support(I^*)\}\) denote the largest possible number of initial infectives that can be proposed in an update.
We now look at the update \((\slower{\ProjEpi}_{n}, \faster{\ProjEpi}_{n}) \mapsto (\slower{\ProjEpi}_{n+1}, \faster{\ProjEpi}_{n+1})\), and shall show that Item 3 holds with 
\[
  \eps \quad=\quad e^{-\beta \TotalRemovals \delta}\, 
  \frac{(\TotalRemovals-1)!}{\Population^{\TotalRemovals-1}} \, 
  \Prob{A_{n+1}} \,
  \Prob{I^*_{n+1} = I^{*,\max}} \quad > \quad 0\,.
\] {#eq-eps-defn}

Given that \(\slower\ProjEpi_{n}\in F_\delta\), any potential removal belonging to \(\slower{\InnovRem}_{\Removal,n+1}\) must lie in the process-time interval \([0,\delta]\); i.e. \(\slower{\InnovRem}_{\Removal,n+1}\) will be a subset of the innovation Poisson process \(\InnovRemMarked{*}_{n+1}[0,\delta]\). Thus we can easily bound the probability that \(\slower{\InnovRem}_{\Removal,n+1}\) is empty:
\[ 
 \Prob{\slower{\InnovRem}_{\Removal,n+1} = \emptyset \,|\, \slower\ProjEpi_{n} \in F_\delta} 
 \quad\ge\quad
  \Prob{\InnovRemMarked{*}_{n+1}[0,\delta] = \emptyset} 
  \quad = \quad
 e^{-\beta \TotalRemovals \delta} \,.
\]
On this event, the coupling of \(\slower{\ProjEpi}\) and \(\faster{\ProjEpi}\) ensures that the set \(\faster{\Pi}^{\text{rem}}_{\Removal,n+1}\) is also empty (see the proof of @thm-update-preserve-ordering), and @lem-update-nfz shows that the no-fly zone boundaries \(\widehat{\nfz}^\infectee_{n+1}\) and \(\slower{\nfz}^\infectee_{n+1}\) both take the value \(-\infty\) on all timelines \(\infectee\). 

Next consider the reassignment of conditioned removals to timelines. 
When we reassign the conditioned removal \(t_\target\), we look at the proposed timeline \(m_\target\) in the innovation \(\InnovResampling^*_{n+1}\): recall that each \(m_\target\) is an independent uniform draw from the set \(\{1,\dots,\Population\}\). 
Since, in both \(\slower{\ProjEpi}_{n}\) and \(\faster{\ProjEpi}_{n}\), the transmission path reaches timeline \(\TotalRemovals\) before process-time \(\delta< t_1\), we know that each timeline \(\target\) must be infectious over the window of process-time \([\delta,t_\target]\). This means that for each \(\target=1,\dots,\TotalRemovals\), _all_ timelines \(\targetm \in\{\target,\dots,\TotalRemovals\}\) are infectious at time \(t_\target\) (since the conditioned removal times are non-decreasing). 
Thus if \(m_\target\in \{\target,\dots,\TotalRemovals\}\), this proposal will be accepted in the update to both \(\slower{\ProjEpi}_{n+1}\) and \(\faster{\ProjEpi}_{n+1}\).

Let \(B_{n+1}\) be the event that in the innovation \(\InnovResampling^*_{n+1}\), \(m_1 = \TotalRemovals\) and \(m_\target\in\{\target,\dots,\TotalRemovals\}\) for \(2\le \target < \TotalRemovals\). As explained above, on the event \(B_{n+1}\), the allocation of conditioned removals to timelines in  
\(\slower{\ProjEpi}_{n+1}\) and \(\faster{\ProjEpi}_{n+1}\) will agree,
with the earliest conditioned removal \(t_1\) assigned to timeline \(\TotalRemovals\).
It follows that 
\[
\begin{aligned}
  &\Prob{t_1 \in \slower{\Pi}^{\text{rem},\TotalRemovals}_{\CRemoval,n+1},\,
		\slower{\overrightarrow\Pi}^{\text{rem}}_{\CRemoval,n+1} =
		\faster{\overrightarrow\Pi^{\text{rem}}_{\CRemoval,n+1}}
		\,|\,
	\slower{\ProjEpi}_n=x \trianglelefteq \faster{x} = \faster{\ProjEpi}_n, x\in F_\delta}
		\\
		& \qquad \ge\quad \Prob{B_{n+1} }
		\quad=\quad  
		\frac{1}{\Population} \prod_{\target=2}^{\TotalRemovals-1} \frac{\TotalRemovals-(\target-1)}{\Population}
      \quad=\quad  
    \frac{(\TotalRemovals-1)!}{\Population^{\TotalRemovals-1}} 
		\,.
\end{aligned}
\]

 We now claim that on the event 
\[
  C_{n+1} = 
  \{\slower{\InnovRem}_{\Removal,n+1} = \emptyset\} \cap
  \{ t_1 \in \slower{\Pi}^{\text{rem},\TotalRemovals}_{\CRemoval,n+1},\,
		\slower{\overrightarrow\Pi}^{\text{rem}}_{\CRemoval,n+1} =
		\faster{\overrightarrow\Pi^{\text{rem}}_{\CRemoval,n+1}}
		\}
		\cap A_{n+1} 
		\cap \{I^*_{n+1} = I^{ *,\max}\}
\]
the laziest feasible epidemics and infection transmission paths in \(\slower{\Epidemic}_{n+1}\) and \(\widehat{\Epidemic}_{n+1}\) must necessarily agree. Recall from @lem-update-lfe that the laziest feasible epidemic \(\slower\lfe_{n+1}\) is composed of infections which either belong to the Poisson process of innovations \(\InnovInfMarkedA{*}_{n+1}\) or which are perpetuated from the transmission path \(\slower\itp_n\). On the event \(C_{n+1}\) the laziest feasible epidemic \(\slower\lfe_{n+1}\) must reach timeline \(\TotalRemovals\) before time \(t_1\), in order to activate that conditioned removal: given that \(\slower{\ProjEpi}_n\in F_\delta\) the path \(\slower{\itp}_n\) reaches timeline \(\TotalRemovals\) during the interval \([0,\delta]\), and on the event \(A_{n+1}\) the Poisson process 
\(\InnovInfMarkedA{*}_{n+1}\) includes a potential infection path from timeline 1 to timeline \(\TotalRemovals\) over the interval \([\delta,t_1)\). 
It follows that _no_ infections belonging to \(\slower{\itp}_n\) will be perpetuated.

Given the coupling between \(\slower\ProjEpi\) and \(\faster\ProjEpi\), exactly the same is true for \(\faster{\ProjEpi}\), and so we see that \(\slower\lfe_{n+1} = \widehat\lfe_{n+1}\). 
We have already observed above that the event \( \{\InnovRemMarked{*}_{n+1}[0,\delta] = \emptyset\}\) forces the no-fly zone boundaries to agree in \(\slower{\Epidemic}_{n+1}\) and \(\widehat{\Epidemic}_{n+1}\), and it follows from @lem-update-itp that the infection transmission paths \(\slower{\overrightarrow\itp}_{n+1}(i_0)\) and \(\widehat{\overrightarrow\itp}_{n+1}(i_0)\) will agree for any given number \(i_0\) of initial infectives. 
Furthermore, when we update the number of initial infectives, the proposed value 
\[
  I^*_{n+1} \quad=\quad I^{ *,\max} \quad\ge\quad \max\{\slower{I}_{0,n}, \faster{I}_{0,n}\}
\]
will be accepted in both \(\slower\ProjEpi\) and \(\faster\ProjEpi\), thanks to @cor-itp-monotonic-in-i0 (remembering once again that on the event \(C_{n+1}\) the no-fly zone boundaries \(\widehat{\nfz}^\infectee_{n+1}\) and \(\slower{\nfz}^\infectee_{n+1}\) both take the value \(-\infty\) on all timelines \(\infectee\)).

Thus, given that \(\slower{\ProjEpi}_n\in F_\delta\) and that \(\slower{\ProjEpi}_n\trianglelefteq\faster{\ProjEpi}_n\), 
on the event \(C_{n+1}\) we get coalescence of \(\slower\ProjEpi_{n+1}\) and \(\faster\ProjEpi_{n+1}\). (We actually get coalescence of the entire epidemic portraits, in fact.) 
Putting this all together we arrive at the following: for all \(\slower{x},\faster{x}\in F_\delta\),
\[
	\Prob{\slower{\ProjEpi}_{n+1} =
      \faster{\ProjEpi}_{n+1} \,|\, \slower{\ProjEpi}_n = x \trianglelefteq \faster{x} = \faster{\ProjEpi}_n} 
	\quad\ge\quad  \Prob{C_{n+1}} \quad\ge\quad\eps\,,
\]
where \(\eps\) was defined in equation (-@eq-eps-defn). In the final calculation here we have made use of the fact that the four events in the definition of \(C_{n+1}\) are determined by independent innovation processes 
(potential removals \(\InnovRemMarked{*}_{n+1}\),
allocation of conditioned removals \(\InnovResampling^*_{n+1}\),
potential infections \(\InnovInfMarkedA{*}_{n+1}\),
and 
proposed update to the number of initial infectives \(I^*_{n+1}\),
respectively).
:::
